interactions.summary: Jiang resets the discussion by distinguishing human free will from angelic function, describing angels as organs of a cosmic body, while students keep pressing the contradiction that Lucifer still seems to have made a decision.

claims.claim: Jiang says humanity's distinctive gift in Paradiso is free will, which sets human beings apart from other orders of being.
Jiang models angels as organs within a body whose task is to maintain the universe rather than to exercise personal free will.
Jiang says Satan's attempt to separate from the body is like an organ becoming cancerous, only to discover that outside the body it has no purpose and simply decays.
Students keep the contradiction alive by insisting that if Lucifer could decide to betray, then some kind of decision-making capacity must have existed despite the no-free-will premise.
A student proposes that Lucifer's exceptional closeness to God's power may explain why he came nearest to betrayal even without ordinary free will.

signature_moments.moment: Lucifer is imagined as an organ that mutates into cancer, gets expelled by the body, and then discovers it cannot live on its own.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Satan chose to become a cancer
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is Jiang's sharpest biological image for rebellion without true autonomy.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's model for angelic beings as differentiated cosmic functions rather than independent choosers.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture now states its working doctrine explicitly: humans have free will; angels are functions. That makes Lucifer's rebellion harder to explain and turns the paradox into a structural feature rather than a mere loose end.

uncertainty_notes.note: The class offers several speculative reconciliations, but none is resolved in this packet.
